answer: I would like to talk about someone whose calm I still try to copy. The most patient person I know is a former teacher of mine, whose calm never seemed to break no matter how testing the situation. She taught us Bengali literature at my higher secondary college in Sirajganj, so I was in her class for two years. Teaching a class of restless teenagers is difficult enough, but she handled even the most disruptive students with remarkable [[composure]]. As for how she showed patience, rather than raising her voice, she would pause, take a breath and respond calmly, which was far more effective. I remember one boy who constantly interrupted her lessons; instead of punishing him, she gave him small responsibilities, and by the end of the year he was one of her best students. What I admired was that her patience was not [[passive]]; it came from genuine understanding of why students behaved as they did. She gave people time to learn at their own pace, never making anyone feel rushed or stupid. I think patience like hers is genuinely [[underrated]], because it requires enormous self-control. Watching her, I realised how much damage impatience can do and how much trust patience can build. Honestly, she has made me consciously try to be more [[tolerant]] in my own daily interactions, though I still have a long way to go. At work, when a student asks me the same question for the fifth time, I often think of her.

followUps.answer: Moderately. I am patient with students and older relatives, but I get rather [[irritable]] in traffic or long queues. It is something I am actively working on, with mixed results so far.

followUps.q: Why do you think people are less patient nowadays?
followUps.answer: Mainly because technology has made everything instant. We are used to fast deliveries and immediate replies, so waiting for anything now feels frustrating, even when the delay is perfectly reasonable.
